newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China sees advance to WTO entry, powers cautious.
newsitem.headline: China sees advance to WTO entry, powers cautious.

text.p: China said Friday it had made major concessions in its decade-long bid to admission to the World Trade Organisation but the United States and other big powers said Beijing still needed to do more.
Trade diplomats said the latest round of discussions had yielded only minor progress, raising doubts that China would join the world trade body by next May, which Beijing had sought.

A senior U.S. official said much more progress was needed for early Chinese entry, and Japanese and European Union envoys said attempts by China to open its markets had fallen short of what other countries expected.
"In the spirit of flexibility and pragmatism, the Chinese delegation has made some new efforts," Beijing's chief WTO negotiator Long Yongtu told negotiators from many of the trade body's 131 members.

At a news conference, he said a pledge of faster openings to key foreign imports like automobiles and electronic products and a commitment to end export subsidies for farm products had been "major contributions" to the negotiations.

Given the sensitivity of the Chinese auto sector, the decision to remove import quotas for foreign cars and minivans over eight to 12 years rather than the 15 originally proposed showed Beijing's "determination to eliminate market access barriers."

The offer to drop support for agricultural exports, a key demand of farming countries in the WTO, had also been difficult but represented a "major contribution" to the world's trading system, Long said.

But U.S. Assistant Deputy Trade Representative Robert Cassidy said that, although some progress had been made in bilateral discussions with the Chinese and the working group meetings, "a lot more needs to be done."
Washington, whose stance Chinese officials consider the main obstacle to entering the global trade body, was looking for a "more comprehensive offer" from Beijing.

This would include a final version of China's market access proposals for reducing tariffs on outside goods and on phasing out non-tariff barriers like quotas, as well as a full offer on access for foreign service providers.

Long, who is also assistant minister for foreign trade, reported that Beijing was working hard on the services package -- originally due by now -- which would be submitted to the WTO by the end of August or early September.
"Until we see that offer, it's impossible to evaluate really where we are," said Cassidy.

His assessment was shared by a Japanese official. "A lot depends on the services offer, but we have been told not to expect too much," said the official. "I have the impression we are just entering the real negotiations," he added.
WTO officials said the next meeting of the working party would be held in October but no date has yet been set.

Diplomats say they expect Beijing to come up with some major advance at that session to prepare for Chinese President Jiang Zemin's visit to Washington for talks with President Clinton at the end of the month.
